story.text: The Iberian lynx wears its identity plainly: a spotted tawny coat, black brushes on the ear tips, a bearded ruff, and a short tail with a black tassel.
It is a specialist to the point of dependence: rabbits are about ninety percent of everything it eats.
When disease crashed the rabbit populations, the lynx crashed with them. By 2002, ninety-four individuals were left.
It was, in those years, the most endangered cat on Earth.
The rescue was unglamorous and total: rabbits restored, private estates enrolled, breeding centers built, road underpasses dug and fenced.
More than four hundred captive-bred lynx have been released into Spain and Portugal since 2010.
Mothers den in hollow cork-oak trunks, shuttling their kittens between hidden bush dens until they emerge at two months.
The 2023 census counted 2,021 lynx — 722 of them cubs.
In June 2024 the IUCN moved it from Endangered to Vulnerable: the greatest recovery of a cat species conservation has ever achieved.
It is not finished — full recovery needs 750 breeding females and the count stands at 406 — but to witness the Iberian lynx is to watch a comeback still gaining ground.

Bottleneck figures kept separate by counting method: 94 total (2002, CINEA) vs 62 mature (2001, IUCN). Lifespan omitted — no verified source. Status is IUCN Vulnerable since June 2024.

stats.size: About 28 lbs · knee-high at the shoulder
stats.diet: European rabbits — about 90% of its diet

reproduction.text: One litter a year, usually around three kittens, born in early spring inside a hollow cork-oak trunk. The mother moves them between hidden bush dens until, at two months, they begin to follow her.

insight.text: The IUCN calls this the greatest recovery of a cat species ever achieved through conservation.
